title: Integrating an LLM Into Your Web App Cheat Sheet

introduction.heading: Sending Your Data to an LLM Safely & Getting Useful Answers Back
introduction.description: A quick reference for wiring an LLM (Claude, GPT, or similar) into a real web app: keeping the API key off the client, shaping your own data into a prompt, asking for structured output you can actually render, and handling the failure modes that come with calling a model instead of a normal API. The running example throughout is a migraine calendar - a user logs symptoms, sleep, stress, and possible triggers over time, and the LLM is asked to look across that log for patterns worth flagging (never a diagnosis, always a correlation) - but the same shape applies to fitness logs, spending trackers, mood journals, or any other data you'd want an LLM to reason over.

prerequisites: A Node.js backend you control (Express or similar) - the LLM is always called from the server, never the browser
An API key for an LLM provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, etc.) with billing set up
A React frontend with some existing user data to analyze (a list of log entries, records, or events)

steps.title: Choose an Architecture: Backend Proxy Only
steps.description: The single most important decision: the browser must never hold your LLM API key. Every request to the model goes browser → your backend → the LLM provider. Your backend is also where you decide what data actually gets sent - the user's whole database, or just the fields relevant to the question.
steps.note: This is the same rule as any other third-party API key (Stripe, SendGrid, ...) - if it can be read from the browser, treat it as already leaked.

steps.title: Install the SDK & Store Your API Key
steps.description: Install the provider's server-side SDK plus a small Express setup, and keep the key in an untracked .env file - the same pattern used for a database connection string.
steps.note: Add a .env.example with a placeholder key so teammates know the variable exists without ever seeing the real value.

steps.title: Create a Minimal Express Proxy Endpoint
steps.description: Start with a route that just proves the wiring works - request in, response out - before adding any LLM logic. Confirms CORS, JSON parsing, and env loading are all correct first.

steps.title: Shape Your Data for the Model
steps.description: Don't hand the model your raw database rows. Pick the fields that matter for the question you're asking, and format them compactly - every extra token costs money and makes the model's job harder, not easier.
steps.note: For a migraine log specifically: pain level, sleep, stress, weather, and self-noted triggers are the signal; internal ids, timestamps down to the second, and unrelated fields are noise - leave them out.

steps.title: Write a Focused System Prompt
steps.description: The system prompt is where you constrain what the model is allowed to say - what counts as evidence, what it must never claim, and exactly what shape the answer should take. Treat it like an API contract, not a suggestion.
steps.note: For anything touching health, finance, or legal topics, explicitly ban diagnostic/causal language ("causes", "you have") in favor of correlational language ("may be associated with") - and say so directly in the prompt.

steps.title: Ask for Structured Output (JSON)
steps.description: Rendering free-form prose in your UI is fragile. Ask the model to respond in a fixed JSON shape (defined in your system prompt) so the frontend can map straight over it, the same way it would map over a normal API response.

steps.title: Parse & Validate the Response
steps.description: Never trust the model's output blindly - strip accidental markdown fences before parsing, wrap parsing in a try/catch, and check the result actually has the shape you asked for before sending it to the client.
steps.note: This is the step most tutorials skip, and the one that turns into a production bug first - a model that's 99% reliable at following a format still fails 1 time in 100.

steps.title: Call the Endpoint from React
steps.description: From the frontend, this is just another fetch to your own backend - no SDK, no API key, no special handling beyond the loading/error states any async request needs.
steps.note: Guard against calling this on too little data - a pattern claimed from 2-3 entries isn't a pattern, it's noise, and the button's disabled state above reflects that.

steps.title: Handle Rate Limits, Caching & Cost
steps.description: LLM calls are slower and more expensive than a normal DB query. Cache results keyed on the data that was analyzed, retry transient failures with backoff, and surface 429s to the user instead of hanging.
steps.note: A cache keyed by a hash of the input data (rather than the user id) is a cheap way to avoid re-analyzing an unchanged log every time someone opens the page.

steps.title: Common Errors & Fixes
steps.description: The errors you'll hit most often when wiring up an LLM call for the first time, and what they actually mean.
steps.note: If the model keeps ignoring the JSON-only instruction, repeat it in the user message as well as the system prompt - and consider a provider's dedicated structured-output/tool-use mode if it has one.

gettingStarted.heading: Getting Started Checklist
steps: Confirm your API key only ever appears in server-side code, never in anything shipped to the browser
Build the Express proxy route and test it with curl before wiring up the frontend
Write a system prompt that fixes both the output JSON shape and what the model isn't allowed to claim
Add try/catch around both the API call and the JSON parsing of its response
Add a loading and an error state to the React component - an LLM call can take several seconds
